pass it on. A little game of lost meaning
Made for curious humans. Bad drawings welcome.Social Graphs · Week 7 ↗
The science under the scribbles

One message.
Three translations.

You turn a real Wikipedia passage into a drawing. The drawing-only route lets a vision model guess directly from its pixels. You can also pass the drawing to a friend, whose short description goes through two text-search systems.

Drawing-only guesses · CLIP
A pretrained image encoder turns the sketch into a normalized 512-dimensional vector. It is compared with vectors from CLIP’s matching text encoder: three fixed descriptions per article, chosen before any drawing is seen. Each article gets its highest candidate cosine. No target ID or human description is supplied to the recognizer. This is retrieval from 303 possibilities, not open-ended caption generation. The image model is 89 MB and runs in a browser worker.
Keyword search · TF-IDF
Compares shared words, giving more weight to terms that are rare in this 303-article corpus. The reveal highlights the actual word contributions.
Semantic search · MiniLM
Encodes your description as a normalized 384-dimensional vector. It ranks articles by cosine similarity to document means or to their best matching passage.
Change the size of the memory
Compare whole-page averages with passages of at most 180 or 60 words. Passage retrieval gives each article the score of its best matching passage. Whole-page vectors average the 180-word passage embeddings, then normalize.
What the score means
A cosine score compares vectors within one method. It is not confidence, a probability, or a percentage of meaning retained. A high score can still retrieve the wrong article.
What this experiment can show
One round is a case study, not a benchmark. Drawings add interpretation; word budgets remove detail. Repeating the game changes more than just word count. Use the same description and switch retrieval units for a controlled comparison.

Source: 303 Wikipedia articles from the course’s frozen August 26, 2026 snapshot. Drawing prompts are exact excerpts with selected names replaced by “someone”; originals and attribution appear at the reveal. Wikipedia text is available under CC BY-SA 4.0.

Text model: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0). Drawing model: CLIP ViT-B/32 (MIT), quantized image and text encoders. Article vectors were prepared with Sentence Transformers; live text queries use the quantized ONNX version of the same encoder in your browser. Stored MiniLM vectors use signed-byte quantization and are renormalized for scoring, so rankings are approximate. TF-IDF uses English stop words, sublinear term frequency, unigrams, and L2 normalization. All models and data are served with this page. Drawings and descriptions stay in this tab; there is no upload or online room.
